newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Q3 growth seen up despite Sept output fall. [CORRECTED 17:06 GMT]
newsitem.headline: German Q3 growth seen up despite Sept output fall. [CORRECTED 17:06 GMT]

text.p: The German economy will post higher, export-led growth in the third quarter despite disappointing industrial output figures in September, economists said on Monday.

Private sector economists are expecting third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) figures, due to be released on Wednesday, to show a year-on-year rise close to the two percent estimated last month by the economics ministry.
Year-on-year growth in the second quarter was 1.2 percent.
Still, some economists said they had revised their outlook for the economy downwards slightly after preliminary industrial output showed a 1.8 percent fall in September.

"The production figures in September were disappointing, and it is becoming clear that one can't expect any pleasant surprises from the consumer climate at the moment," Bank Julius Baer chief economist Gerhard Grebe said.
Grebe said he had originally been forecasting third-quarter growth of one percent compared to the previous quarter, but had now revised that down to 0.7 percent, for 1.7 percent year-on-year growth.
The quarter-on-quarter growth figure is in any case seen well below the 1.5 percent posted in the second quarter.

Other economists added they were disappointed that a subsequent revision of the industrial output data reduced the headline fall by less than many economists expected, (corrects from "left the headline fall unchanged").

"Even so, that leaves industrial production growth at around 1.2 percent for the quarter, which would imply around a half-percent rise in quarter-on-quarter (GDP)," Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt said.
Mayer forecasts a two percent year-on-year GDP rise for the third quarter.
Strong exports, boosted by the weaker mark, are widely seen as the main factor behind third-quarter growth.
"These figures will clearly be export-driven," said Industrial Bank of Japan economist Adolf Rosenstock, who forecasts year-on-year growth of 1.8 to 1.9 percent in the quarter.
He added that the figures would show a cyclical recovery that first took hold in spring was continuing, though at a less dramatic rate than past post-recession recoveries.
Rosenstock said he thought it likely that economic growth could take a pause in the next two quarters, as a winter lull and weakness in east German sectors such as construction had an effect.
"But with next spring, we should see a further upswing lasting for the rest of the year -- assuming investment starts to pick up," he added.
Rosenstock said he saw good signs from a recent survey from the Ifo economic research institute showing a gain in business confidence, but said more proof was still needed.
